subject: OpenAI halved its API price 90 minutes after Anthropic
bodyMarkdown:
Two of the biggest AI labs cut their prices within ninety minutes of each other yesterday afternoon. If your employer pays for AI by the query, or you are still deciding whether to start, the arithmetic changed while you were asleep.

## Two price cuts, ninety minutes apart

Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on Tuesday at $4 per million input **tokens**, the chunks of text a model reads and writes, metered the way a utility meters kilowatt hours, and $20 per million output tokens. Opus 5 cost $5 and $25, so that is a 20 per cent cut, and cached reads fell further, from 50 cents per million to 20. Then OpenAI answered. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna arrived about ninety minutes later, with Sol at $2 and $10, half of what Anthropic had just announced and half of what GPT-5.6 Sol charged. Luna is 10 cents in and 50 cents out. CNBC reported on Tuesday that these were the first releases from either company since the two labs joined calls to slow AI development down. The slowdown, I notice, did not extend to price.

## The cost of thinking keeps falling

This did not start yesterday. CNBC reported on September 1 that the LLM Token Expenditure Index from Silicon Data, which tracks what the market actually pays for a million tokens across all models, had fallen to 97 cents, the lowest since the index began late last year and less than half its level earlier in the summer. The awkward part for the labs is that they raised enormous sums on the premise that **inference**, the business of running a finished model for a paying customer, would stay a high margin business. A 50 per cent cut only survives that premise if the cost of serving a token is dropping faster than the price, and none of these companies publish that number. OpenAI says the new rates are permanent rather than promotional. That is a real commitment, and I think it is aimed squarely at everyone building on its API.

## Canada is buying this, slowly

Statistics Canada reported that 19.2 per cent of Canadian businesses used AI to produce goods or deliver services in the second quarter, up from 12.2 per cent a year earlier and 6.1 per cent in 2024. That survey ran from April 1 to May 6 and drew 9,251 responses. The spread by industry is wide: information and cultural industries came in at 42.3 per cent, agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting at 4.5. All of it was collected before yesterday, and before most of this year's price drops. From watching small firms around Richmond Hill try this, my view is that the licence fee was never the barrier that mattered. Finding one person who knows what to point the thing at costs far more than the tokens do. Cheaper tokens still help, because they make a failed experiment cost almost nothing.

## The takeaway

If you buy AI through an API, reprice your workloads this week, because a model you rejected in July on cost may clear the bar now. Check whether your vendor passes the cut through or quietly keeps it, since the coding assistants and support tools sitting on top of these APIs just got a margin windfall they did not earn. I am watching for the first provider to raise a price instead of cutting one, which is the signal that somebody's compute bill finally caught up. The next Statistics Canada reading on business AI use will tell us whether cheap tokens actually moved that 19.2 per cent.
